summary: Defines two MIB modules for managing MAC bridges. One covers the traffic classes and enhanced multicast filtering of IEEE 802.1D, and the other covers VLANs as specified in IEEE 802.1Q. It supplements RFC 4188, obsoletes RFC 2674, and is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: A network switch is a bridge: it connects LAN segments below the IP layer. VLANs let one physical network act as several separate logical networks, and traffic classes let a switch treat urgent and routine traffic differently. This RFC defines the SNMP objects for reading and changing those settings on a switch.

subtitle: The SNMP management objects that let you configure a network switch's traffic priorities, multicast filtering and VLANs.

tldr.problem: The BRIDGE-MIB of RFC 4188 covers the basic transparent bridge, but not the traffic class and enhanced multicast filtering of IEEE 802.1D-1998, and not the VLANs of IEEE 802.1Q-2003, which switched LANs depend on.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two MIB modules. P-BRIDGE-MIB covers traffic classes, priority mapping, GARP and GMRP and restricted group registration. Q-BRIDGE-MIB covers VLAN configuration, the per-VLAN forwarding database, static entries, port VLAN parameters and the protocol classification tables.
tldr.outcome: A manager can read and configure the priorities, multicast filtering and VLANs of a bridge through standard SNMP objects. The RFC supplements RFC 4188 and obsoletes RFC 2674.

today: RFC 4363 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2006. It obsoletes RFC 2674 and supplements RFC 4188, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Two MIB Modules for Bridges
sections.content:
The memo defines two MIB modules for managing the capabilities of MAC bridges defined by the IEEE 802.1D-1998 MAC Bridges standard and the IEEE 802.1Q-2003 Virtual LAN standard for bridging between Local Area Network segments. One module defines objects for managing the Traffic Classes and Enhanced Multicast Filtering components of IEEE 802.1D-1998 and P802.1t-2001. The other defines objects for managing VLANs, as specified in IEEE 802.1Q-2003, P802.1u and P802.1v. Provisions are made for support of transparent bridging, and also so that these objects apply to bridges connected by subnetworks other than LAN segments. The memo supplements RFC 4188 and obsoletes RFC 2674.

Section 1 places the modules in the Internet-Standard Management Framework and points to Section 7 of RFC 3410 for a detailed overview. The modules are compliant to SMIv2, described in STD 58, RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.

Section 2 gives the background. A common device present in many networks is the bridge, used to connect LAN segments below the network layer; these devices are often known as layer 2 switches. The transparent method of bridging is defined by IEEE 802.1D-1998, and managed objects for transparent bridging are defined in the BRIDGE-MIB of RFC 4188.

The original IEEE 802.1D is augmented by IEEE 802.1Q-2003 to provide support for virtual bridged LANs, where a single bridged physical LAN network may be used to support multiple logical bridged LANs, each of which offers a service approximately the same as that defined by IEEE 802.1D. Such VLANs are an integral feature of switched LAN networks. A VLAN can be viewed as a group of end stations on multiple LAN segments that can communicate as if they were on a single LAN. IEEE 802.1Q defines port-based VLANs, where membership is determined by the bridge port on which data frames are received, and port-and-protocol-based VLANs, where membership is determined by the bridge port and the protocol identifier of the frame. This memo defines the objects needed for the management of port-based VLANs in bridge entities.
sections.plainLanguage: A network switch is a bridge: it connects LAN segments below the IP layer. VLANs let one physical network act as several separate logical networks, and traffic classes let a switch treat urgent and routine traffic differently. This RFC defines the SNMP objects for reading and changing those settings on a switch.

sections.title: What Was Left Out and Why
sections.content:
The MIB modules include a comprehensive set of managed objects that attempts to match the set defined in IEEE 802.1D and IEEE 802.1Q. However, to be consistent with the spirit of the SNMP framework, a subjective judgement was made to omit the objects from those standards most costly to implement in an agent and least essential for fault and configuration management.

The RFC records the historical principles the original BRIDGE-MIB of RFC 1493 used to decide inclusion. Start with a small set of essential objects and add only as further objects are needed. Require that objects be essential for either fault or configuration management. Consider evidence of current use and utility. Limit the total number of objects. Exclude objects that are simply derivable from others in this or other MIBs. And avoid causing critical sections to be heavily instrumented, following the guideline of one counter per critical section per layer.

Section 3 explains the structure. The P-BRIDGE-MIB module defines managed objects for the traffic class and multicast filtering enhancements defined by IEEE 802.1D-1998, including the Restricted Group Registration control defined by IEEE P802.1t. The Q-BRIDGE-MIB module defines managed objects for the Virtual LAN bridging enhancements defined by IEEE 802.1Q-2003, including the Restricted VLAN Registration control defined by IEEE P802.1u and the VLAN Classification by Protocol and Port enhancement defined by IEEE P802.1v.

Section 3.1.1 lists the objects from IEEE 802.1D-1998 that were left out. The Bridge.StateValue object was not considered useful. The Bridge.ApplicantAdministrativeControl object is not provided per attribute, for example per VLAN or per group; only per device, port and application control is provided in this MIB. The notify group registration failure object of IEEE 802.1t was not considered useful.

Section 3.1.1 also explains a placement decision. Some objects defined by IEEE 802.1D-1998 have been included in the virtual bridge MIB module rather than the extended one: entries in dot1qTpGroupTable, dot1qForwardAllTable and dot1qForwardUnregisteredTable are required for virtual bridged LANs with additional indexing, for example per VLAN and per filtering database, so they are not defined in the extended module. Devices that do not implement virtual bridged LANs but do implement the Extended Forwarding Services defined by IEEE 802.1D should implement these tables with a fixed value for dot1qFdbId or dot1qVlanIndex, for which the value 1 is recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC tries to cover the standards closely, but it leaves out the objects that would be expensive for a device to implement and least useful for finding faults or changing configuration. It also explains that some multicast forwarding tables live in the VLAN module rather than the plain bridge module, because in a VLAN network the same table has to be indexed by VLAN as well as by port.

sections.title: The Subtrees of the Extended Bridge MIB
sections.content:
Objects in the P-BRIDGE-MIB are arranged into subtrees, each organized as a set of related objects, and the RFC gives the assignment of objects to subtrees. The dot1dExtBase subtree holds the objects applicable to all bridges implementing the traffic class and multicast filtering features of IEEE 802.1D-1998, including per-device configuration of the Generic Attribute Registration Protocol, GARP, and the GARP Multicast Registration Protocol, GMRP. It includes dot1dDeviceCapabilities, which reports dot1dExtendedFilteringServices and dot1dTrafficClasses, and dot1dTrafficClassesEnabled.

The dot1dPriority subtree holds the objects for configuring and reporting the status of priority-based queuing mechanisms in a bridge: per-port user priority treatment, the mapping of user priority in frames into internal traffic classes, and outbound user priority and access priority. Its tables are dot1dPortPriorityTable, with dot1dPortDefaultUserPriority and dot1dPortNumTrafficClasses; dot1dUserPriorityRegenTable, with dot1dUserPriority and dot1dRegenUserPriority; dot1dTrafficClassTable, with dot1dTrafficClassPriority and dot1dTrafficClass; and dot1dPortOutboundAccessPriorityTable.

The dot1dGarp subtree holds the objects for configuring and reporting on the operation of GARP, in the dot1dPortGarpTable with the join, leave and leave-all times. The dot1dGmrp subtree holds the objects for GMRP, in the dot1dPortGmrpTable, including dot1dPortGmrpStatus, dot1dPortGmrpFailedRegistrations, dot1dPortGmrpLastPduOrigin and dot1dPortRestrictedGroupRegistration, which reflects the Restricted Group Registration control of IEEE 802.1t.

Two further tables extend the dot1dTp subtree of the BRIDGE-MIB. The dot1dTpHCPortTable reports port-bridging statistics for high-capacity network interfaces, and the dot1dTpPortOverflowTable reports the upper bits of those statistics for when 32-bit counters are inadequate.
sections.plainLanguage: The first module is split into five groups. One holds the device-wide settings, including which features the switch supports. One holds the priority settings: the priority a port assigns to arriving traffic, the map from that priority to the switch's internal traffic classes, and the priority used when sending traffic out. Two hold the multicast registration protocols GARP and GMRP. The last two hold port statistics, one of them for high-capacity interfaces whose counters do not fit in 32 bits.

sections.title: The Subtrees of the Virtual Bridge MIB
sections.content:
Some manageable objects defined in the BRIDGE-MIB need to be indexed differently when they are used in a VLAN bridging environment, so they are effectively duplicated by new objects with different indexing, which are defined in the Q-BRIDGE-MIB. Unlike IEEE 802.1D-1998, IEEE 802.1Q-2003 did not define exact syntax for a set of managed objects, so the RFC's cross-references give the section numbering of the management operation descriptions from clause 12 of that standard.

The dot1qBase subtree holds dot1qVlanVersionNumber, dot1qMaxVlanId, which is the maximum IEEE 802.1Q VLAN-ID the device supports, dot1qMaxSupportedVlans, the maximum number of VLANs the device supports, dot1qNumVlans, and dot1qGvrpStatus.

The dot1qTp subtree holds the transparent bridging tables. dot1qFdbTable carries dot1qFdbId and dot1qFdbDynamicCount, the number of entries in the filtering database that were learned dynamically. The dot1qTpFdbTable holds a row for each unicast MAC address for which the device has forwarding or filtering information, indexed by dot1qFdbId and dot1qTpFdbAddress, and each row gives the port, the status and the VLAN. The dot1qTpGroupTable holds group entries with the group address, its egress ports and whether it was learnt. The dot1qForwardAllTable and dot1qForwardUnregisteredTable give the ports to which all traffic, and traffic from unregistered sources, may be forwarded, split into static and forbidden ports.

The dot1qStatic subtree holds the permanent entries. dot1qStaticUnicastTable gives, for each static unicast address, the receive port and the ports it is allowed to go to. dot1qStaticMulticastTable gives the equivalent for multicast, with the static egress ports and the forbidden egress ports.

The dot1qVlan subtree holds the VLAN configuration itself. dot1qVlanCurrentTable has a row per VLAN currently in use, with dot1qVlanIndex, the filtering database identifier dot1qVlanFdbId, dot1qVlanCurrentEgressPorts, the set of ports transmitting traffic for this VLAN as tagged or untagged frames, dot1qVlanCurrentUntaggedPorts, the subset transmitting untagged frames, the status and the creation time. The dot1qVlanStaticTable holds the configured VLANs, with the name, the egress ports, the forbidden egress ports, the untagged ports and a row status. dot1qPortVlanTable holds the per-port settings: dot1qPvid, the port's default VLAN, dot1qPortAcceptableFrameTypes and dot1qPortIngressFiltering. dot1qLearningConstraintsTable holds the constraints on how VLANs may be learned, and dot1qVlanNumDeletes counts VLAN deletions.

A fifth subtree, dot1vProtocol, holds the VLAN Classification by Protocol and Port tables of IEEE P802.1v, namely dot1vProtocolGroupTable, dot1vProtocolPortTable and dot1vProtocolVlanTable.
sections.plainLanguage: The VLAN module has five groups. One holds the device-wide facts, such as how many VLANs the switch supports. One holds the forwarding tables: which MAC addresses the switch has learned, which group addresses it knows, and where traffic may be sent. One holds the permanent, hand-configured entries. One holds the VLANs themselves: which ports belong to each VLAN, which ports may send untagged traffic, and the per-port default VLAN. The fifth holds the protocol classification tables.

sections.title: How the Modules Fit with the Other MIBs
sections.content:
Section 3.4 describes the relationship to other MIB modules, and Section 3.4.3 gives recommendations for devices implementing these enhancements. The dot1dBase subtree of the BRIDGE-MIB holds the device-wide objects, the dot1dStp subtree holds the spanning tree objects, the dot1dTp subtree holds the transparent bridging tables and the dot1dStatic subtree holds the permanent entries. The additions in this memo extend the dot1dTp subtree with the two high-capacity statistics tables and the dot1dTpHCPortTable.

Section 3.4.1 covers the relationship to the SNMPv2-MIB, and Section 3.4.2 the relationship to the IF-MIB. The IF-MIB relationship is broken into three parts. The layering model describes how the bridge ports map onto interface rows. The ifStackTable section describes how the bridge ports relate to the physical interfaces below them. The ifRcvAddressTable section covers the receive addresses.

Section 3.3 defines the textual conventions the modules use, and Section 3.4.3 records the recommendations for using the BRIDGE-MIB objects on devices that implement the enhancements defined here.
sections.plainLanguage: The two modules are designed to sit on top of the ordinary bridge MIB rather than replace it. The bridge ports are related to the physical interfaces of the switch through the standard interface stacking table, so a manager can walk from a VLAN's port list down to the interface it belongs to.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A number of management objects defined in the MIB modules have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write or read-create, and such objects may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. The RFC states that support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations.

In the P-BRIDGE-MIB, the objects dot1dTrafficClassesEnabled, dot1dGmrpStatus, dot1dPortPriorityTable, dot1dUserPriorityRegenTable, dot1dTrafficClassTable, dot1dPortGarpTable and dot1dPortGmrpTable can be manipulated to interfere with the operation of priority classes. This could be used to force a reinitialization of state machines, thus causing network instability, or to override established policy on port priorities, giving a user or an attacker unauthorized preferential treatment.

In the Q-BRIDGE-MIB, the objects dot1qGvrpStatus, dot1qForwardAllTable, dot1qStaticUnicastTable, dot1qStaticMulticastTable, dot1qVlanStaticTable, dot1qPortVlanTable, dot1qLearningConstraintsTable, dot1vProtocolGroupTable and dot1vProtocolPortTable could be manipulated to interfere with the operation of virtual LANs, in the same way, or by changing the forwarding and filtering policies.

Some of the readable objects may also be considered sensitive, and the RFC says it is thus important to control even GET and NOTIFY access to them, and possibly to encrypt their values when sending them over the network. The dot1dDeviceCapabilities and dot1dPortCapabilitiesTable objects in the P-BRIDGE-MIB could be used by an attacker to determine which attacks might be useful against a given device. In the Q-BRIDGE-MIB, the read-only objects dot1qMaxVlanID, dot1qMaxSupportedVlans, dot1qNumVlans, dot1qFdbTable, dot1qTpFdbTable, dot1qTpGroupTable, dot1qVlanCurrentTable and dot1qPortVlanStatisticsTable could be used to determine which attacks might be useful, to detect whether attacks are being blocked or filtered, or to understand the logical topology of the network.
sections.plainLanguage: Several of these objects can be written, and a wrong value can destabilize the switch or change which traffic goes where, so anyone who can write them can give themselves preferential treatment. Even reading them is sensitive, because the tables reveal which addresses the switch has learned and how the network is wired together.
